name: Napoleon Hill
tagline: A promoter of many failed schemes who wrote a best-selling book on desire and persistence.
startedFrom: He was born Oliver Napoleon Hill in 1883 in the hills of Wise County, Virginia, and his mother died when he was nine. He later called his family three generations of 'ignorance, illiteracy and poverty', but his grandfather was a printer and his father a self-taught dentist. His stepmother made him go to school and bought him a typewriter, and as a boy he wrote news items for rural newspapers.

evidence.claim: Fortune's review of his 1995 biography says no one ever sought success more desperately than Hill, and that he floated some 30 ventures, nearly all of them doomed.
evidence.locator: paragraph beginning 'No one ever sought success more desperately than Hill'

evidence.claim: In 1928, broke, he borrowed money from his brother-in-law, rented a large hotel suite in Philadelphia to look successful, and persuaded the publisher Andrew Pelton, whom he did not know, to bring out his eight-volume Law of Success.
evidence.locator: paragraphs beginning 'Sometime in late 1927 or early 1928' and 'Hill was completely broke in Philadelphia'

evidence.claim: The first of his six steps for turning desire into money is to fix in your mind the exact amount of money you want; it is not enough, he writes, to say 'I want plenty of money'.
evidence.locator: ch. 2 'Desire: The Starting Point of All Achievement', the six steps

evidence.claim: When the royalties from Law of Success reached about $2,500 a month in 1929, he spent them on fine clothes, a Rolls-Royce and a 600-acre estate in the Catskills.
evidence.locator: paragraphs beginning 'But Hill was ever distilling his laws of success' and 'As fast as the money rolled in'

evidence.claim: Publishers Weekly says he spent most of his life jumping from one get-rich-quick scheme to another and lived through long periods of poverty.
He writes that persistence is to the character of man what carbon is to steel.
evidence.locator: ch. 9 'Persistence: The Sustained Effort Necessary to Induce Faith', opening pages

evidence.claim: After the Depression cost him his Catskills estate and his royalties dried up, he kept going with his 'Mental Dynamite' lecture series and by editing and writing Inspiration Magazine, and in 1937 he published Think and Grow Rich.
evidence.locator: paragraphs beginning 'As fast as the money rolled in', 'Unbowed, Hill scrabbled a living' and 'IN 1937'

evidence.claim: Fortune says financial security eluded him until he was well into his sixties, and that all the while he lectured on success.
evidence.locator: paragraph beginning 'No one ever sought success more desperately than Hill'

evidence.claim: He writes that the imagination is literally the workshop where all plans made by man are shaped.
evidence.locator: ch. 6 'Imagination: The Workshop of the Mind', first sentence

evidence.claim: His biographers, quoted by Novak, say his boyhood news writing was crude but made up for it with 'a vivid imagination', and that he later recalled simply making stories up when news was scarce.
evidence.locator: paragraph beginning 'So Napoleon started writing for a small weekly newsletter' and the biographers' quotation after it

evidence.claim: In the early 1920s, between ventures, he founded another periodical carrying advertisements for organizations of his own invention, among them the Peptomists and the Co-Operative Club.

principles.text: Decide exactly what you want, what you will give for it and by when; write it down with a plan and read it aloud every night and morning.
principles.locator: ch. 2 'Desire: The Starting Point of All Achievement', the six steps

principles.text: Treat a defeat as a sign that your plan was wrong: rebuild the plan and keep going.
principles.locator: ch. 7 'Organized Planning', paragraph beginning 'When defeat comes'

principles.text: Make decisions quickly and change them slowly.
principles.locator: ch. 8 'Decision: The Mastery of Procrastination', opening paragraphs

principles.text: Do not let other people's opinions make your decisions; share your plans only with the few allies you have chosen.
principles.locator: ch. 8 'Decision', paragraphs beginning 'Opinions are the cheapest commodities on earth' and 'Keep your own counsel'

principles.text: For any large goal, work with a small group of people in harmony toward one definite purpose.
principles.locator: ch. 10 'Power of the Master Mind', section 'Gaining Power through the Master Mind'

quotes.text: There may be no heroic connotation to the word "persistence," but the quality is to the character of man what carbon is to steel.
quotes.locator: ch. 9 'Persistence: The Sustained Effort Necessary to Induce Faith', opening pages

quotes.text: When defeat comes, accept it as a signal that your plans are not sound, rebuild those plans, and set sail once more toward your coveted goal.
quotes.locator: ch. 7 'Organized Planning: The Crystallization of Desire into Action', paragraph beginning 'When defeat comes'

quotes.text: Men who succeed reach decisions promptly, and change them, if at all, very slowly.
quotes.locator: ch. 7 'Organized Planning', 'The Thirty Major Causes of Failure', no. 13 'Lack of a well defined power of decision'

quotes.text: The imagination is literally the workshop wherein are fashioned all plans created by man.
quotes.locator: ch. 6 'Imagination: The Workshop of the Mind', first sentence

definingMoment.text: In 1936, aged 53, divorced and without money, he married Rosa Lee Beeland after meeting her at one of his lectures in Knoxville, Tennessee. The couple moved into his son Blair's small New York apartment, and by his biographers' account she typed and edited his manuscript through at least three complete rewrites. His old publisher, Andrew Pelton, at first doubted there was still a market for such a book in the Depression, but agreed to print it. Think and Grow Rich came out in 1937; by 1995 Fortune counted more than ten million copies sold.

shadow.text: Newspaper and court records gathered by the journalist Matt Novak (2016) show him in trouble over money again and again: in 1908 he fled Mobile, Alabama, after his lumber company bought lumber on credit and sold it cheaply for cash, and in 1918 warrants were issued against him in Chicago under the Illinois law on selling stock. In 1923 an Ohio prison warden told a local newspaper that the money Hill had collected for a prisoners' correspondence school never arrived. At about 15 he married a girl who was expecting a child, after her father demanded it; by his 1995 biographers' account, quoted by Novak, she then said the child was not his and the marriage was annulled. No source found gives her age. In her 1908 divorce petition his second wife, Edith, accused him of threatening to kill her and of choking their small daughter. Publishers Weekly, reviewing the 1995 biography, says he deserted his wife and children several times and left their support to others; Novak names her as his third wife, Florence, who divorced him in 1935. The New York Times review of the same book says that as a young employee of a coal-mine owner he arranged to have the death of a Black bellhop in an accidental shooting involving the drunk mine manager covered up, and was made manager of the mine, at 19, as a reward; later, after losing his magazine to some of his employees, he denounced one of them to the F.B.I. as a German agent. He claimed that Andrew Carnegie gave him his life's mission in 1908 and that he advised Presidents Wilson and Roosevelt; Carnegie's biographer David Nasaw told Novak he found no evidence the two men ever met, and Fortune notes Hill also called himself an attorney, which he was not.

councilQuestion.text: Which decision did you put off this week, and what kept you from making it?

screen.notes: A real American self-help author (1883-1970), not fictional, never a politician in office (only claimed a 'race' for Congress around 1915-17), not the founder of a religion, and with no account found of sexual contact with anyone under 16 or of sexual violence; he is in, with a large documented dark side: repeated fraud charges and flights from creditors, money collected for prisoners that never arrived, a wife's 1908 divorce petition alleging violence to her and their small daughter, desertion of his family, and invented claims about Carnegie, Wilson and Roosevelt. His first marriage, at about 15, was to a girl who was expecting a child; her father demanded the marriage, she then said the child was not his, and it was annulled (Ritt and Landers 1995, quoted by Novak 2016). No source found gives her age, so it is not an owner case on the record; it is told in the shadow.

review.devilsAdvocate: I attacked each value against the 1939 Ralston scan of Think and Grow Rich, Novak's archival account (2016) and the four 1995 reviews of his biography. Partnership fell: his partners in lumber, the Automobile College, the Mount Vernon Inn and the Betsy Ross Candy Shop left, sued or pushed him out, three wives left him or divorced him, and the Stone partnership soured by the early 1960s, so only the narrow sense of collaborating on a book or a business survives. Ambition, Wealth and Determination held as core values shared with the blind pick, and Imagination held on his own chapter, Novak and the New York Times; all four quotes match the 1939 printing. The shadow now adds his annulled first marriage at about 15 (her age unknown), the 1903 mine cover-up and the F.B.I. denunciation, and one fact on Inspiration Magazine was corrected.
